clue.text: Marxist Mrs Gargery ? That shows a dangerous spirit

parts.note: a Marxist is a communist, a Red
in Dickens's Great Expectations Joe Gargery's second wife is Biddy

explanation.surface: A Dickens character turned revolutionary proves a menace.
explanation.walkthrough: Red biddy is a cheap drink of red wine laced with methylated spirits, hence 'dangerous'. Joe Gargery marries Biddy at the end of Great Expectations.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names rough wine fortified with meths, a spirit drunk by down-and-outs that could poison.

clue.text: Cloth fashionable, school public

parts.note: rep is a ribbed fabric
ton means fashion or fashionable society

explanation.surface: Smart fabric worn publicly at school.
explanation.walkthrough: Repton is an English public school, meaning a fee-paying independent school, in Derbyshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Repton is one of England's old fee-paying boarding schools, which the British call public schools.

clue.text: The Bill of New York

parts.note: reads like a police force or a law, but a bill here is a banknote used in New York

explanation.surface: Looks like a reference to a police force or a piece of law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Bill' is British slang for the police, which steers you away from the American banknote.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call a banknote a bill, and the basic unit of US currency is this.

clue.text: Where are those Spaniards? Mostly here, Drake

definitions.text: Where are those Spaniards? Mostly here, Drake

parts.words: Where are those Spaniards? Mostly here, Drake
parts.note: Spanish ships sailed the Spanish Main where Drake raided them, and the phrase also means mostly

explanation.surface: Sir Francis Drake is told where to find the Spanish enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spanish Main was the Caribbean coast and sea that Drake plundered; the phrase also means 'for the most part'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means generally or for the most part, and the main was the open sea of Spanish treasure fleets.

clue.text: Who pulled the brewer's dray of course

definitions.text: Who pulled the brewer's dray of course

parts.words: Who pulled the brewer's dray of course
parts.note: a heavy cart animal pulled the brewery wagon, and draught also means beer on tap

explanation.surface: Asks the obvious about who hauled the beer cart.
explanation.walkthrough: Draught means both hauling and beer drawn from the cask, so the brewery's cart horse fits doubly.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy horse bred to haul loads is so called, and brewers' wagons were drawn by them.

clue.text: Free for King George, as it might be

parts.note: GR is Georgius Rex, the royal cipher of King George

indicators.note: the words as it 'might be' something else, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gift to the monarch, perhaps, costing nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: GR is followed by ATIS, the anagram of AS IT signalled by 'might be'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something given gratis costs nothing, so it is free of charge.

clue.text: Game though groggy

explanation.definitionFit: A card game of melding sets; and an old adjective for drunk or befuddled, from rum.

clue.text: That'll do' for now

parts.note: the words fill the phrase 'for ... ', which as a whole means for now

explanation.surface: Someone calls a halt for the present.
explanation.walkthrough: Put 'for' before the answer and you get an old idiom meaning for the present.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom with 'for' in front means for the time being, a single occasion.

clue.text: Though furiously incensed don't be blind to a fact

definitions.text: don't be blind to a fact

explanation.surface: Even in a rage, face the truth.
explanation.definitionFit: Boiling with rage describes it; split in two, it is an order to notice an item.

clue.text: Chum, at lunch-hour meet Alphonse in the " Grand "

parts.note: a chum is a pal
lunch is taken at one o'clock, and one is the Roman numeral I
Al is the short form of Alphonse, as in Al Capone

explanation.surface: Meeting a friend for lunch at the Grand hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: The lunch hour is one o'clock, giving I for one. 'meet' and 'in the' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A palatial building is splendid and imposing, as grand as a palace.

clue.text: Mum turns to Goriot for -current reading

indicators.note: turns tells us the word for Mum is read backwards

parts.note: Mum is Ma
Balzac's novel is Le Pere Goriot, Father Goriot

explanation.surface: A mother takes up Balzac's novel for some reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' reverses MA to AM; Goriot is Pere (father) in Balzac's title. 'to' and 'for' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Electric current is measured in units of this name, so a meter's reading of current is given in them.

clue.text: Thermal quality of a particular eliminatory event?

explanation.definitionFit: Physics measure of heat needed to warm a unit mass by one degree; also a precise qualifying race, a heat.

clue.text: Stand up and cheer like Humpty Dumpty ?

explanation.surface: Applauding a nursery-rhyme figure on his wall.
explanation.definitionFit: To give an ovation is to applaud, often on one's feet; and an egg-shaped thing, like the nursery-rhyme egg, is oval.

clue.text: Chichester insect

explanation.definitionFit: Sir Francis Chichester flew and sailed vessels of this name; it is also a European moth whose caterpillars strip trees.

clue.text: Is it what makes " Home. Sweet Home " so moving?

definitions.text: Is it what makes " Home. Sweet Home " so moving?

parts.words: Is it what makes " Home. Sweet Home " so moving?
parts.note: moving reads not as touching but as house removal: the large van that carries a household's furniture

explanation.surface: Asks what makes the sentimental song so touching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' pretends to mean emotional; the vehicle in mind is a furniture removal van.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an old word for a big lorry used by removal firms to shift a family's belongings.

clue.text: In turn with a cipher sum up an apocryphal gospeller

indicators.note: turn says the word In is read backwards

parts.note: a cipher is a code

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word sum is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Adding up a coded message about a lost gospel writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In turn' gives NI; 'sum up' gives MUS. 'with a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A noncanonical gospel is attributed to this Pharisee who visited Jesus by night.

clue.text: Bone-setter gives a shiver ?

explanation.definitionFit: One who splints broken limbs; and a sliver or fragment, as a shiver is.

clue.text: In life and on the line they have their class distinctions

definitions.text: In life and on the line they have their class distinctions

parts.words: In life and on the line they have their class distinctions
parts.note: social ranks in life and railway stops both come in classes

explanation.surface: Comments on the English class system.
explanation.walkthrough: One's station in life is social rank; railway stations once had first and third class waiting rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means social positions and also stopping places on a railway line.

clue.text: Where children of necessity are taken for protection

definitions.text: Where children of necessity are taken for protection

parts.words: Where children of necessity are taken for protection
parts.note: necessity is the mother of invention, so its children are inventions, brought to be safeguarded by patents

explanation.surface: Sounds like a refuge for needy children.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'necessity is the mother of invention' makes inventions her children; inventors register them to protect their rights.
explanation.definitionFit: Inventors file at this government bureau to secure exclusive legal rights over their designs.

clue.text: Toll for " Eight-month " French monarch?

parts.note: October was the eighth month of the Roman year, abbreviated Oct
roi is French for king

explanation.surface: Paying a tax for a short-reigning king of France.
explanation.walkthrough: OCT is October, named as the eighth month in the old Roman calendar.
explanation.definitionFit: An old local duty levied on goods entering a French town is called by this name.

clue.text: Rotter for whom a young cleric might have had a good word

definitions.text: for whom a young cleric might have had a good word

explanation.walkthrough: In a Punch cartoon a curate, served a stale egg, says it is good in parts: the curate's egg.
explanation.definitionFit: A scoundrel is so called; and the curate's egg, told to his bishop, was 'good in parts'.

clue.text: R.C. inn: it is essential for a change

indicators.note: the letters of the fodder are given a change of order

explanation.surface: A Catholic hostelry is a necessary novelty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for a change' rearranges the letters of RC INN IT IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Intrinsic qualities belong to a thing's basic nature, so they are inherent and fundamental.

clue.text: In Olympian vein

parts.note: the fluid running in the veins of the gods of Olympus

explanation.surface: Sounds like a remark about grand style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vein' pretends to mean manner; read literally it is the blood vessel of a god.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the ethereal fluid flowing through gods' veins in place of blood.

clue.text: Had a chat, bare-headed in a Russian villa

indicators.note: the opening of the phrase is stripped off, leaving letters from inside it

explanation.surface: Chatting hatless in a country house in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the head H from 'Had a chat' and take the run that follows, stopping before the final T.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian country cottage or summer house is called by this name.

clue.text: Overmuch your dentures showing

parts.note: overmuch means too
thy is the old form of your

explanation.surface: Your false teeth are on display too much.
explanation.walkthrough: THY is the archaic word for 'your'.
explanation.definitionFit: A grin that shows a lot of teeth is described this way, with the dentures on display.

clue.text: Orpheus did but not Eurydice

parts.note: in the Greek myth the musician came back up from the underworld, but his wife was lost when he looked back

explanation.surface: Contrasts the fates of the mythical lovers.
explanation.walkthrough: Orpheus led Eurydice from Hades but turned to look at her too soon, so only he came out again.
explanation.definitionFit: To come out again into the open is what Orpheus did on leaving Hades.

clue.text: A lot of blooms are beaded

explanation.surface: Flowers in a garden appear covered in beads of dew.
explanation.definitionFit: A rose garden is a plot of flowers; and a string of prayer beads carries this name, so it is the beaded thing.

clue.text: Hiding a store of shag tins, maybe

indicators.note: maybe says the words could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Someone hides tins of pipe tobacco.
explanation.walkthrough: Shag is a coarse cut pipe tobacco sold in tins; 'maybe' rearranges SHAG TINS. 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To stash is to hide a hoard away, so putting a store out of sight is this.
